# Analysis — drivers, trend and coverage

**Generated by** `src/analyse.py` (`make analyse`) · **dataset**
`data/clean/feedback_classified.parquet`, 7,150 rows, 5,353
with a comment · **thresholds** from `config.yaml`, committed before any result (gate G7) ·
**run provenance** `reports/run_manifest.json`.

This file is the working paper. `reports/business_report.md` quotes from it and every number
there appears here with its denominator and its row count. Nothing in this file is a
decision; the decisions are in `DECISIONS.md`.

**The four rules this analysis runs under**, each from a Wave 4 result and each enforced in
code rather than in the prose:

| | Rule | Decision |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | The customer's star rating is the primary signal. Sentiment (kappa 0.403 against a floor of 0.6) appears only as a labelled method comparison | D-055, D-065 |
| 2 | Theme negative *rates* are reportable with 44.1% model–owner agreement stated; theme *rankings* are not. Theme tables are alphabetical | D-065, D-066 |
| 3 | No theme × department × dealership cut. Two-way nationally; theme × dealership for the sites that clear the floor; five thin sites at department level | D-060 |
| 4 | Every rate names its denominator — all 7,150 rows, or the 5,353 commented ones | D-058 |

---


## 1. The headline, with its denominator

The primary signal is the customer's own star rating (D-065). The sentiment model missed
the pass mark committed in D-055 — Cohen's kappa **0.403** against a floor of
**0.6** — and the star rating scored **0.46** on the same 150 blind
labels, so the rating is both the committed fallback and the better-measured signal.

| Measure | Count | Denominator | Rate |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Negative by rating (1–2) | 1,609 | all 7,150 rows | **22.5%** |
| Negative by rating (1–2) | 1,504 | the 5,353 commented rows | **28.1%** |
| Negative by D-004 (rating 1–2 *or* sentiment negative) | 2,131 | all 7,150 rows | 29.8% |
| Sentiment-negative *(method comparison, kappa 0.403)* | 1,641 | the 5,353 commented rows | 30.7% |

**Which number to quote, and why it matters.** The two rating rows differ by
**5.6 percentage points** off the same data. Commented rows average
**3.54** stars and commentless rows **4.40** — satisfied customers tick
five and leave, dissatisfied ones write — so the commented subset is not a sample of the
feedback population (D-058). *"28% of feedback is negative"* is
true only of the 5,353 rows that carry a comment. Across everything Kestrel collected
the figure is **22.5%**.

Every table below names its denominator in its caption for the same reason.

## 2. Drivers — by department

`department` is a hand-mapped field: 16 source spellings reduced to three, every mapping
approved by the owner (D-048, D-049, D-050). It is not model output, so unlike the themes
in section 4 these three rows **can** be compared with each other.

**Denominators:** the rating columns are over all 7,150 rows; the last two columns are
over the commented subset only.

| Department | rows (all) | negative by rating | rate % of all rows | 95% CI | mean rating | commented rows | rate % of commented | sentiment-negative % of commented |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Service | 4,903 | 1,333 | 27.2 | 26.0–28.5 | 3.57 | 3,743 | 33.3 | 34.8 |
| Parts | 706 | 113 | 16.0 | 13.5–18.9 | 3.95 | 508 | 20.9 | 26.8 |
| Sales | 1,541 | 163 | 10.6 | 9.1–12.2 | 4.26 | 1,102 | 13.9 | 18.3 |

Service carries **4,903 of 7,150 rows (68.6%)** and the worst
rate on either denominator. Sales and Parts are each under a fifth of the volume. Whatever
is wrong, most of it is in the service lane — and that conclusion needs no theme model and
no sentiment model to reach it.

## 4. Drivers — by theme, and what may not be said about them

> **The 44.1% caveat.** Of the 143 comments the owner placed in a theme when labelling
> blind, the model placed **44.1%** in the same theme (D-065,
> `reports/evaluation.md`). Theme assignment is embedding similarity to eight owner-approved
> themes with no confidence floor, because the floor was tested against those labels and
> did not separate the comments the owner rejected from the ones they kept (D-066).
>
> **A theme's negative rate is reportable with that figure attached. One theme ranked above
> another is not.** This table is printed in **alphabetical order** for that reason, and no
> figure in `reports/business_report.md` rests on the order of these eight rows.

**Denominator:** the 5,353 commented rows only — a theme cannot be assigned to a row
with no comment, and D-057 gives those rows a null theme rather than a guessed one. These
rates are therefore not comparable with the all-rows rates in sections 2 and 3.

| Theme | comments | % of commented rows | negative by rating | rate % of this theme | 95% CI | mean rating | sentiment-negative % |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | --- | ---: | ---: |
| Booking | 369 | 6.9 | 164 | 44.4 | 39.5–49.5 | 2.98 | 42.0 |
| Communication and updates | 802 | 15.0 | 310 | 38.7 | 35.3–42.1 | 3.16 | 39.7 |
| Explanation and transparency | 398 | 7.4 | 113 | 28.4 | 24.2–33.0 | 3.58 | 31.2 |
| Parts availability | 368 | 6.9 | 159 | 43.2 | 38.2–48.3 | 2.98 | 43.2 |
| Pricing and billing | 686 | 12.8 | 165 | 24.1 | 21.0–27.4 | 3.63 | 28.1 |
| Staff manner | 1,395 | 26.1 | 120 | 8.6 | 7.2–10.2 | 4.23 | 12.2 |
| Waiting and turnaround | 881 | 16.5 | 275 | 31.2 | 28.2–34.4 | 3.45 | 33.5 |
| Workmanship and rework | 454 | 8.5 | 198 | 43.6 | 39.1–48.2 | 2.98 | 50.0 |

**What survives the caveat.** Two things, both of which hold without any theme being ranked:

1. **Staff manner is the largest theme and the least negative of the eight by a wide
   margin** — 8.6% against
   a 28.1% rate across all commented rows. A 44%
   reliable classifier placing 1,395 comments cannot be trusted on *which* operational
   theme a comment belongs to, but the staff/operations distinction is the coarsest cut in
   the list and the one it is least likely to be wrong about.
2. **The rating-based and sentiment-based columns agree on the shape** — the two right-hand
   columns track each other across all eight rows despite being built from different
   signals. That is corroboration of the *pattern*, not of the ordering, and it comes with
   sentiment's own kappa of 0.403 attached.

The 20 failure cases in `reports/llm_review.md` show why: the recurring comment in this
corpus praises the people and complains about the process — *"Great welcome, helpful staff.
Problem not fixed."* Those comments are negative, and which operational theme they land in
is exactly what the 44.1% is uncertain about.

## 7. The trend — has anything changed over the year?

### 7.1 The committed rule, and what it finds

D-052 set the evidence rule **before any trend result existed** (gate G7), from the measured
SD of 1.44 in `reports/trend_evidence.md`:

| Setting | Committed value | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `min_month_responses` | **20** | a change between two 20-response months carries ±0.46 of noise |
| `min_change_1to5` | **0.5** | sits just outside that band |
| `thin_dealer_basis` | **quarterly** | NSW07, QLD05, QLD07, VIC08, VIC09 have a median month under 20 |

Applied to this dataset, the rule finds **33 of 256 consecutive
dealer-month pairs** at **16 of 24 sites**.

> **Reconciled against the committed evidence file**, which predicted 33 of **257** at 16 of
> 24 from the 7,159 pre-validation rows. The flag count and the site count match exactly.
> The pair count does not, and the reason is a single known gap: `scripts/trend_evidence.py`
> paired each month with the previous *present* month, so Penrith (NSW02) had its May 2026
> paired with its July 2026 across the missing June — the sheet D-029 excluded as a copy of
> July. This module requires the two months to be adjacent, which drops that one pair.
> 257 − 1 = 256. Nothing else differs.

**And the site-level rule finds no direction: 16 of the 33 moves are
downward and 17 upward.** That symmetry is the honest result of the rule at the grain it
was calibrated for, and it is why the trend claim in 7.2 is not made from this table.

4.09 → 2.62 stars, a fall of

### 7.2 The trend that is real: the group declined over the year

**This is the §2 non-negotiable trend, and it is a group-level claim, not a site-level one.**

| month | responses | mean rating (all 24) | negative rate % (all 24) | mean rating (excl VIC09) | negative rate % (excl VIC09) |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 2025-10 | 614 | 3.824 | 20.5 | 3.824 | 20.6 |
| 2025-11 | 567 | 3.862 | 19.2 | 3.868 | 19.0 |
| 2025-12 | 552 | 3.944 | 17.4 | 3.932 | 17.5 |
| 2026-01 | 516 | 3.725 | 22.3 | 3.71 | 22.8 |
| 2026-02 | 594 | 3.907 | 18.0 | 3.908 | 17.9 |
| 2026-03 | 614 | 3.787 | 22.0 | 3.791 | 22.0 |
| 2026-04 | 603 | 3.642 | 27.0 | 3.642 | 27.0 |
| 2026-05 | 618 | 3.714 | 23.6 | 3.714 | 23.6 |
| 2026-06 | 612 | 3.614 | 26.5 | 3.614 | 26.5 |
| 2026-07 | 616 | 3.724 | 22.9 | 3.724 | 22.9 |
| 2026-08 | 620 | 3.589 | 27.1 | 3.589 | 27.1 |
| 2026-09 | 624 | 3.744 | 22.6 | 3.744 | 22.6 |

Split at the midpoint of the twelve months — which is also the month the closed site shut,
so the boundary is given by the data rather than chosen to maximise the gap:

| | H1 (Oct 2025 – Mar 2026) | H2 (Apr – Sep 2026) | Change |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Responses | 3,457 | 3,693 | |
| Mean rating | **3.842** | **3.671** | **-0.171 stars** |
| Negative rate, all rows | **19.9%** | **24.9%** | **+5.0 pts** |
| Excluding VIC09 (D-005) | 3.840 / 20.0% | 3.671 / 24.9% | -0.169 / +5.0 pts |

**Why this is evidence and not noise, judged by D-052's own arithmetic.** The committed
0.5-star threshold is calibrated for a *dealership-month* pair at n = 20, where
the 1-sigma noise band is ±0.46. The same formula — `sd × √(1/n₁ + 1/n₂)` — at this grain,
with n = 3,457 against 3,693 and the dataset's SD of
1.44, gives a noise band of **±0.034 stars**. The observed
fall of 0.171 is **5.0×**
that band.

Stating it the other way round, so the threshold is not quietly discarded: the group's
0.171-star fall is **well below** D-052's 0.5-star floor and would not
qualify as a movement *at a single site in a single month*. It qualifies here because it is
measured on 3,457 responses against 3,693 instead of forty, and the rule
is a function of n, not a constant. Three independent tests agree:

| Test | Statistic | p |
|---|---|---|
| Welch t-test on the ratings | t = 5.037 | **4.9e-07** |
| Mann–Whitney U (no normality assumption) | — | **1.6e-05** |
| χ² on the negative/not-negative counts | — | **4e-07** |

**With and without the closed site (D-005).** VIC09 closed on 31 March 2026, so all
52 of its rows sit in H1 and its disappearance
is exactly the composition change D-005 was written to catch. Removing it moves the fall
from -0.171 to -0.169 and the Welch p from
4.9e-07 to 7.3e-07. The trend is not the closure.

**Three robustness checks, because an aggregate can move for reasons that are not the thing
being measured, and then the same test run inside each department:**

| Check | H1 | H2 | Verdict |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Department mix changed? | Parts 9.6% / Sales 21.1% / Service 69.3% | Parts 10.2% / Sales 21.9% / Service 67.9% | No — mix is stable, so the fall is not composition |
| Response volume changed? | 3,457 rows | 3,693 rows | No — within 7%, and 12 near-equal months (section 7.2) |
| Commenting propensity changed? | 72.5% left a comment | 77.1% left a comment | Yes, +4.6 pts — consistent with more dissatisfaction (D-058), and the rating series above is over ALL rows so it is unaffected |
| Where is it? Service | 3.671 stars, 24.0% neg (n=2,395) | 3.468 stars, 30.2% neg (n=2,508) | -0.204 stars, +6.21 pts, p = 1.8e-06 |
| Where is it? Sales | 4.345 stars, 8.2% neg (n=731) | 4.178 stars, 12.7% neg (n=810) | -0.167 stars, +4.51 pts, p = 0.0043 |
| Where is it? Parts | 3.970 stars, 16.0% neg (n=331) | 3.939 stars, 16.0% neg (n=375) | -0.031 stars, -0.01 pts, p = 0.75 |

### 7.3 Where the decline actually is: NSW, and three named sites

The group figure in 7.2 is true and it is also an average over three states that did
different things. Splitting it is the first thing a reader should do with it.

**By state.** Denominator: all rows in that state, by rating.

| State | Sites | Rows | H1 rating | H2 rating | Change | H1 neg % | H2 neg % | Neg change (pts) | Welch p | Change excl VIC09 |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | --- | ---: |
| NSW | 7 | 2,243 | 3.946 | 3.616 | -0.33 | 18.1 | 26.4 | 8.3 | 7.9e-08 | -0.33 |
| VIC | 9 | 2,693 | 3.813 | 3.648 | -0.166 | 20.5 | 25.1 | 4.6 | 0.0028 | -0.159 |
| QLD | 8 | 2,214 | 3.773 | 3.758 | -0.015 | 21.0 | 23.3 | 2.2 | 0.8 | -0.015 |

**The decline is overwhelmingly NSW: -0.330 stars and +8.3 points of negative rate (p = 7.9e-08), against VIC's -0.166 and QLD's -0.015 (p = 0.8) — which is no change at all.** QLD is flat on both measures and its Welch test does not come close to
significance. A single group number reported without this split would have told
Queensland's sites they had a problem they do not have, and understated NSW's by more than
half.

Inside NSW the deterioration is in the customer-facing lanes, not in Parts:

| Department | Rows | H1 neg % | H2 neg % | Change (pts) | Rating change | Welch p |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | --- |

**By site, with the multiple-comparison problem handled rather than ignored.** Testing 23
sites for a change produces false positives by construction: at p < 0.05 roughly one site in
twenty turns up "significant" with nothing happening. The Holm step-down correction is
applied across all 23 tests, and the column to read is the adjusted one. Sites with fewer
than 20 responses in either half are not tested at all (D-052's floor).

| VIC09 | VIC | Shepparton | 52 | 3.98 | — | — | — | not tested (n < floor) |

**3 of 23 sites survive the correction, and every one of them is a fall.** No site
improved significantly. That asymmetry is itself evidence: random variation across 23 sites
would not produce 3 one-sided results.

**Which tests are corrected, and which are not.** The Holm family above is the 23 per-site
tests and only those. The three state tests and the three NSW department tests in this
section, and the three national department tests in 7.2, are **uncorrected Welch p-values** —
nine in all. They are not part of the site family and are not presented as a screen, but a
reader who notices the care taken over 23 tests is entitled to ask about the other nine. The
two load-bearing ones survive any correction comfortably: a Bonferroni factor of 9 leaves NSW
at 7e-07 and NSW Service at 2.8e-06. The marginal ones do not change character either
(VIC 0.0028 → 0.025, NSW Sales 0.00068 → 0.0062). **No conclusion in this report rests on an
uncorrected p-value.** Raised by the independent verifier (V-4).

This is the full extent of the per-site testing in this project. Cut-list item 7 makes
statistical tests beyond the one trend check cuttable, and the one kept here is the one the
recommendation needs — *which* sites, not *whether* something changed.

## 8. Coverage — how much of the business this dataset sees

**Reported as a limitation (D-006), and it is also the floor under every number above.**

| | Transactions, Oct 2025 – Sep 2026 | Feedback rows | Coverage |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Service jobs | 200,249 | 4,903 | **2.45%** |
| Vehicles sold | 16,011 | 1,541 | **9.62%** |
| Parts transactions | 62,437 | 706 | **1.13%** |
| **All three** | **278,697** | **7,150** | **2.57%** |

**What this does and does not undermine.** Every rate in this report is a rate *among
customers who responded*, and 2.57% of transactions produced a
response. Nothing here establishes what the other 97.4%
think, and D-058's evidence points the wrong way for optimism: within the responses, the
ones who wrote are markedly less satisfied than the ones who did not, so response is not
independent of satisfaction. The correct reading of
*"22.5% of responses are negative"* is a rate over
7,150 responses out of 278,697 transactions, and not a rate over Kestrel's
customers.

## 9. Does any of it reach the revenue? — the honest answer is "not measurably"

**This section exists because the question has to be asked**: are these customers acting on
their dissatisfaction, or complaining without consequence? `monthly_revenue.csv` is the only
behavioural data in the project — 288 dealer-months of service jobs, vehicle
sales, parts transactions and the dollars attached to each. **The finding is a null result,
and it is reported as one.**

### 9.1 The raw correlation points the wrong way, and that is the first lesson

Across all 281 dealer-months, a site's negative rate correlates **positively** with its
service volume: **r = +0.218, p = 0.00024**. Read naively that says complaints
*cause* business.

They do not. Big sites have more service jobs and more feedback for reasons that have nothing
to do with satisfaction, and comparing Chermside with Noosa measures size, not sentiment.
Removing each dealer's own average and each month's national average — so the only variation
left is **one site against its own baseline, in a month compared with that month everywhere
else** — flips the sign:

| Comparison | r | p |
|---|---:|---:|
| Raw, across sites *(confounded by site size)* | **+0.218** | 0.00024 |
| **Within site and month — service jobs** | **-0.186** | **0.0018** |
| **Within site and month — service revenue** | **-0.175** | **0.0032** |

So within a site, a month with a higher-than-usual negative rate is also a month with
lower-than-usual service volume. The effect is small: **-8.1 service jobs per
10 percentage points of negative rate** (95% CI -13.1 to
-3.1), against a mean of 709 jobs — about
**-1.1%** of a typical dealer-month.

### 9.2 But it is a same-month association, not a leading indicator

This is the test that decides the business question. If dissatisfaction drove customers away,
this month's negative rate would predict **next** month's volume. It does not:

| Lag (months) | What it tests | r | p | dealer-months |
| --- | --- | ---: | --- | ---: |
| -3 | service jobs 3 months BEFORE the feedback | 0.096 | 0.166 | 209 |
| -2 | service jobs 2 months BEFORE the feedback | -0.067 | 0.312 | 233 |
| -1 | service jobs 1 month BEFORE the feedback | -0.075 | 0.231 | 257 |
| 0 | same month | -0.186 | 0.002 | 281 |
| +1 | service jobs 1 month AFTER the feedback | -0.106 | 0.091 | 257 |
| +2 | service jobs 2 months AFTER the feedback | -0.038 | 0.566 | 233 |
| +3 | service jobs 3 months AFTER the feedback | -0.069 | 0.319 | 209 |

**The association is strongest at lag 0 and is not significant at any lag in either
direction.** Nothing about a bad month at a site tells you anything about its volume one,
two or three months later. A same-month association is just as consistent with "a month when
the branch is struggling produces both fewer completed jobs and more complaints" as with any
story about customers leaving — and this analysis cannot separate those.

### 9.3 The natural experiment, and it comes out flat

Section 7.3 found that NSW's negative rate rose 8.3 points while Queensland's did not move.
That is the closest thing to a controlled comparison this dataset offers: **if dissatisfaction
costs volume, NSW should have lost ground against QLD.**

| State | Service jobs H1→H2 | Service revenue H1→H2 | Vehicles sold H1→H2 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| NSW | +4.9% | +4.8% | +7.3% |
| VIC | +6.2% | +5.2% | +7.8% |
| QLD | +6.6% | +5.9% | +9.9% |

**NSW's satisfaction collapsed and its service volume grew — by 4.9%.**

The ordering is in the direction the hypothesis predicts: NSW, which fell furthest, grew
least; QLD, which did not move, grew most; VIC sits between them on both. That is worth
stating because it is the one piece of evidence in this section that points *towards* a
link, and leaving it out would be the convenient omission.

**It does not survive being tested.** Comparing per-site growth, NSW averages
+5.1% against QLD's +6.6% — a difference of
-1.5 percentage points with **p = 0.41** on 7 sites
against 8. A gap that size arises by chance roughly two times in five. Three states ordered
correctly is also the weakest possible evidence: with three groups there is a one-in-six
chance of any particular ordering appearing at random. The direction is suggestive; the
magnitude is indistinguishable from nothing.

The same test on the three sites whose own rating fall survived correction:

| Dealer | Rating fall | Service jobs H1 | Service jobs H2 | Change |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: | --- |
| NSW01 | −0.75 | 6,214 | 6,051 | -2.6% |
| VIC01 | −0.72 | 6,083 | 6,096 | +0.2% |
| NSW04 | −0.58 | 3,653 | 4,001 | +9.5% |
| the other 20 open sites | none significant | 80,342 | 85,881 | +6.9% |

One lost volume, one was flat, and one grew faster than the group. **Three sites, no
pattern.**

### 9.4 What this null result is worth, and what it is not

**It is not "negative feedback has no consequences".** It is "this dataset cannot detect
one", and the distinction matters because three separate things could produce the same
flat result:

1. **Twelve months is probably too short.** A service interval is six to twelve months. A
   customer who gave up on Parramatta in April 2026 may simply not have been due back before
   the data ends in September. Churn of this kind would appear *after* the window, not in it.
2. **The monthly negative rate is a noisy instrument.** A median dealer-month carries
   25 responses, so the sampling error on its negative rate is
   about ±8 points. Only **33%** of the month-to-month variance in the
   measured rate is real signal; the rest is sampling noise. That attenuates every
   correlation above toward zero — the observed -0.186 corresponds to a true value
   nearer **-0.322** once corrected.
3. **The relationship may genuinely not be in this data.** The challenge pack is fictional.
   If its revenue figures were generated independently of its feedback, no amount of analysis
   will find a link that was never put there — and the flat result above is exactly what that
   would look like.

**What the null result does establish.** With 281 dealer-months the panel could detect a
correlation of **|r| ≥ 0.166** at 80% power, and no lagged correlation came close.
So a *large* month-to-month effect of satisfaction on near-term service volume is ruled out
by this data. A small one, or a slow one, is not.

**The consequence for the value question.** D-025 asked for a dollar figure built on external
benchmarks. This section is the internal check on whether such a figure would mean anything,
and it says: **Kestrel's own twelve months of revenue show no measurable link between
satisfaction and near-term customer behaviour.** Publishing a dollar value derived from
published retention benchmarks, while the client's own data declines to corroborate the
mechanism those benchmarks assume, would be the least defensible number in the project. This
strengthens the decision to cut the value model rather than weakening it (section 11).

**What would answer the question properly:** customer-level repeat-visit data — did the
individual who left a 1-star in April come back? The dataset has no customer identifier by
design (D-003), so this project cannot ask that question and no amount of analysis here will
change that. It is the single most valuable thing Kestrel could add to the next round of
this work.

### 9.5 One data-quality finding, for free

`monthly_revenue.csv` records **exactly zero** service jobs, vehicle sales and parts
transactions for VIC09 in all six months from April 2026. The feedback data and the
revenue file were produced separately, so this is **independent corroboration of the closure
date in D-005** rather than an assumption carried between them. Those six months are dropped
from every correlation above; left in, they would enter as six extreme outliers.


## 10. Where to focus first — the analysis behind the recommendation

**The recommendation is argued from volume, the rating and coverage. It is not argued from a
theme ranking**, because D-065 does not permit one.

| Step | Number | Where it comes from |
|---|---:|---|
| 1. **What** — Service is most of the feedback | 4,903 of 7,150 rows (**68.6%**) and 71.9% of the transactions behind it | section 2, hand-mapped department field |
| 2. **What** — Service has the worst rate on either denominator | **27.2%** of its 4,903 rows | section 2 |
| 3. **When** — it got worse over the year | 24.0% → 30.2% negative (**+6.2 pts**, p = 1.8e-06) | section 7.2 |
| 4. **Where** — the decline is NSW, not the group | NSW **-0.330** stars (p = 7.9e-08) · VIC -0.166 · QLD **-0.015, p = 0.8** | section 7.3 |
| 5. **Where** — NSW Service is the specific cell | 21.7% → 32.1% negative (**+10.3 pts**, p = 3.1e-07) on 1,473 rows | section 7.3 |
| 6. **Who** — three sites survive multiple-comparison correction | **Parramatta** (NSW01, -0.75), **Dandenong** (VIC01, -0.72), **Liverpool** (NSW04, -0.58) — all falls, no site improved | section 7.3 |
| 7. **How much is seen** — very little | service coverage **2.45%** — one response per ~41 service jobs | section 8 |

**The chain.** Service holds 68.6% of the feedback and
71.9% of the transactions behind it, and has the worst negative rate of
the three departments on both denominators — that is the standing problem, and it is the
same in all three states. **What changed this year is narrower than the group figure
suggests.** Splitting the group's +5.0-point move by state gives NSW
+8.3, VIC +4.6 and QLD
+2.2 with a Welch p of 0.8 — Queensland did not
change. Inside NSW the move is **+10.3 points in Service** and
+8.5 in Sales, while NSW Parts went the other way.

In plain counts, the national Service move is **156 more negative service responses in
H2 than H1's rate would have produced**.

**So the recommendation has two parts that should not be confused.** The *standing* problem
is Service everywhere. The *new* problem is NSW, and specifically
**Parramatta** (NSW01, -0.75 stars) and **Liverpool** (NSW04, -0.58 stars) — the two NSW sites whose own change survives Holm correction across 23
tests. Dandenong (VIC01) is the third and sits outside NSW, so it belongs with them on
evidence even though the state story does not reach it.

**What is deliberately not published here.** 156 responses at a 2.45% response
rate would extrapolate to roughly 6,341 service jobs. That figure is **not** reported as
a finding, because D-058 measured response bias running the wrong way for it — within the
responses, the people who wrote are markedly less satisfied than the people who did not — so
projecting a responder rate onto all 200,249 jobs would overstate it by an unknown amount.
The defensible version of the volume argument is the one above: Service is where both the
feedback and the business sit, and the decline is in Service.

**Why the theme evidence is supporting and not load-bearing.** Section 4 shows staff manner
is both the largest theme and by a wide margin the least negative, and the 20 adjudication
failure cases in `reports/llm_review.md` are almost all the same shape — the people are
praised and the process is not: *"Great welcome, helpful staff. Problem not fixed."*,
*"nice helpful staff, wait was too long tho"*. That points at process rather than people,
which is a useful steer for where to look inside Service. It is a steer and not a finding:
at 44.1% model–owner theme agreement, *which* process is uncertain even where
the staff/process split is not.

**What is not here.** The third business question asks roughly what it is worth. D-025 is
unset and `reports/benchmarks.md` is unreviewed, so no dollar figure is published. Section 9
is the internal check on whether such a figure would mean anything; see also section 11.

## 11. Limitations, and the one question this report does not answer

1. **No dollar value (D-025 unset).** PLAN.md section 1 asks "roughly what is it worth".
   `reports/benchmarks.md` exists but **the owner has not reviewed it**, and the benchmarks
   themselves state that no published source maps a 1–5 satisfaction rating to dollars. Any
   figure here would be a scenario presented as a measurement, so the value model is cut
   under the brief's step 6 and the cut list's first item. The business report says so
   explicitly rather than leaving a gap.
2. **Sentiment missed its pass mark** — kappa 0.403 against 0.6
   (D-065). Every figure in this report that could be built from the rating is built from
   the rating. Sentiment appears only beside a rating-based figure, labelled.
3. **Theme assignment agrees with the owner 44.1% of the time** (D-065), with no
   confidence floor because the floor did not work (D-066). Theme rates are reportable;
   theme rankings are not, and nothing in section 9 depends on one.
4. **The three-way drivers cut does not exist** (D-060). Theme × department is national;
   theme × dealership covers 19 of 24 sites.
5. **2.57% coverage, and response is not independent of
   satisfaction** (sections 8, D-006, D-058). The 5,353 commented rows average 3.54 stars
   against 4.40 for the 1,797 commentless ones.
6. **One trend test, not a battery.** Cut-list item 7 makes tests beyond the one trend check
   cuttable; section 7.2 runs three tests on the one claim rather than many claims with one
   test each. No seasonality model: twelve months cannot separate a seasonal cycle from a
   decline, and this report does not try.
7. **Sarcasm is a measured weakness** in the sentiment column (D-063): 15.2% of comments
   carry Australian slang markers and all eight polarity-inverted pilot cases were irony.
   The LLM's 45.5% sarcasm rate over its 857-comment scope is unvalidated model output
   (D-017) and is not quoted as a measurement anywhere in either report.
8. **This analysis was not independently reproduced.** Checkpoint 5's independent verifier
   (D-017, producer ≠ checker) had not run at the time of writing. Every number above comes
   from `src/analyse.py` over committed inputs, so `make analyse` reproduces them; that is
   reproducibility, not independence.
